title: Truthiness of 0
code: puts 0 ? "yes" : "no"
explanation:
Only nil and false are falsy in Ruby.

0 ? "yes" : "no"  # => "yes"
"" ? "yes" : "no" # => "yes"
[] ? "yes" : "no" # => "yes"

Python and JavaScript treat 0 as falsy. Ruby does not.

title: Array.new with a default object
code:
a = Array.new(3, [])
a[0] << 1
p a
explanation:
All three slots share one [] object:

a = Array.new(3, [])  # [[], [], []] — same object in every slot
a[0] << 1             # mutates that one array
# a is now [[1], [1], [1]]

Use Array.new(3) { [] } for a fresh array per slot.

title: Symbol and string keys
code:
h = { "name" => "Ada" }
p h[:name]
explanation:
"name" and :name are different keys.

h = { "name" => "Ada" }
h[:name]   # => nil   — missing key, not a misspelling
h["name"]  # => "Ada"

Hash#[] returns nil for a missing key. Hash#fetch would raise KeyError.

title: ||= on false
code:
enabled = false
enabled ||= true
p enabled
explanation:
a ||= b assigns when a is falsy. false is falsy, so it gets replaced:

enabled = false
enabled ||= true  # same as enabled = enabled || true
# enabled is now true

Do not use ||= to default a boolean that may legitimately be false.

title: return inside a block
code:
def find_big
  [1, 2, 3].each { |x| return x * 10 if x == 2 }
  :none
end
p find_big
explanation:
return inside a block returns from the enclosing method, not just from the block.

[1, 2, 3].each { |x| return x * 10 if x == 2 }
# when x == 2, this exits find_big with 20
# :none is never reached

title: << mutates a shared string
code:
a = "hi"
b = a
b << "!"
p a
explanation:
a and b are the same String object. << mutates it in place:

a = "hi"
b = a       # b is a, not a copy
b << "!"    # mutates that one string
# a is now "hi!"

b += "!" would build a new string and leave a as "hi".

title: Integer division
explanation:
Dividing two Integers gives an Integer, rounded toward negative infinity — not toward zero.

-7 / 2    # => -4   (not -3)
7 / 2     # => 3

Make one side a Float (-7 / 2.0 or -7.fdiv(2)) to get -3.5.

title: Spot the local variable
prompt: Which line assigns a local variable?
code:
1  $flag = true
2  class Box
3    @label = "x"
4    def pack
5      size = 1
6      @size = size
7    end
8  end
explanation:
size on line 5 is a local.

1  $flag = true   # global
3  @label = "x"   # class instance variable (on Box itself)
5  size = 1       # local
6  @size = size   # instance variable of each Box

title: Spot the instance variable
prompt: Which line assigns an instance variable of each object?
code:
1  class Box
2    @@n = 0
3    def initialize(name)
4      @name = name
5      tag = :ok
6    end
7  end
explanation:
@name on line 4 lives on each Box instance.

2  @@n = 0        # class variable, shared by the class
3  initialize(name)  # name is a local (the parameter)
4  @name = name   # instance variable of each Box
5  tag = :ok      # local

title: Spot the class variable
prompt: Which line assigns a class variable?
code:
1  class Box
2    @@n = 0
3    @n = 0
4    def reset
5      @n = 0
6    end
7  end
explanation:
@@n is the class variable. The two @n assignments are different objects:

2  @@n = 0   # class variable, shared by Box and its subclasses
3  @n = 0    # class instance variable, on Box itself
5  @n = 0    # instance variable of each Box object

title: Spot the class instance variable
prompt: Which line assigns a class instance variable?
code:
1  class Box
2    @@n = 0
3    @n = 0
4    def reset
5      @n = 0
6    end
7  end
explanation:
@n in the class body sits on the Box object, not on instances.

2  @@n = 0   # shared class state (Box and subclasses)
3  @n = 0    # class instance variable — this is the one
5  @n = 0    # instance variable of each Box, a different @n

title: Spot the global variable
prompt: Which line assigns a global variable?
code:
1  count = 0
2  $count = 0
3  class App
4    @count = 0
5  end
explanation:
$count is global.

1  count = 0    # local
2  $count = 0   # global
4  @count = 0   # class instance variable of App

title: Spot the symbol
code:
1  name = "Ada"
2  key = :ada
3  $key = name
4  @key = key
explanation:
:ada is a Symbol.

1  name = "Ada"  # String
2  key = :ada    # Symbol
3  $key = name   # global, still holding a String
4  @key = key    # instance variable (of main at top level)

title: Parameters are locals
prompt: Which line introduces the local variable `name`?
code:
1  $name = "x"
2  class User
3    def initialize(name)
4      @name = name
5    end
6  end
explanation:
A method parameter is a local. Line 3 is where name comes into scope.

1  $name = "x"           # a different, global name
3  def initialize(name)  # introduces the local
4  @name = name          # reads that local into an instance variable

title: Quoted hash label
explanation:
The quotes on line 2 are a label, not a String key. That label still becomes a Symbol:

{ "id" => 1 }  # String key "id"
{ "id": 1 }    # same as { id: 1 } — key is :id
{ id: 1 }      # also :id

Line 3's id is a local Integer. Line 4 uses that integer as the key.

title: Constants that look global
prompt: Which line reads a global variable?
code:
1  p ARGV
2  p $0
3  p ENV["PATH"]
4  p STDIN
explanation:
ARGV, ENV and STDIN are constants, not globals. $0 is a global (the program name).

ARGV         # constant, the argument Array
$0           # global
ENV["PATH"]  # constant, the environment Hash
STDIN        # constant (related to $stdin, which is the global)

title: Class variables and subclasses
prompt: Which line is shared with subclasses?
code:
1  class Animal
2    @@legs = 4
3    @kind = "x"
4  end
5  class Dog < Animal
6    def kind
7      @kind
8    end
9  end
explanation:
@@legs is one variable for Animal and Dog together.

2  @@legs = 4   # shared class variable — this is the one
3  @kind = "x"  # class instance variable, only on Animal
7  @kind        # Dog's instance variable, a third name

title: and vs &&
code:
x = true and false
p x
explanation:
and binds looser than assignment. The line is (x = true) and false, so x stays true.

x = true and false  # => (x = true) and false
# x is true

x = true && false   # => x = (true && false)
# x would be false

Use && / || in expressions. Use and / or for control flow.

title: Hash.new with a default object
code:
h = Hash.new([])
h[:a] << 1
p h
explanation:
h[:a] returns the shared default array without storing it under :a. << mutates that default; the hash stays empty.

h = Hash.new([])
h[:a] << 1  # mutates the default, does not write :a
p h         # => {}
h[:b]       # => [1]  — same default array

Use Hash.new { |hash, k| hash[k] = [] } to store a fresh array per key.

title: return inside a lambda
code:
def wrap
  f = -> { return 20 }
  f.call
  :none
end
p wrap
explanation:
return in a lambda leaves only the lambda. wrap keeps going.

f = -> { return 20 }
f.call   # => 20, back in wrap
:none    # this still runs

A block's return would have exited wrap with 20. Lambdas do not.

title: === is not symmetric
code: p [Integer === 1, 1 === Integer]
explanation:
=== is case-equality. Integer === 1 asks "is 1 an Integer?" The other way around, Integer is not an Integer instance.

Integer === 1  # => true   — used by case/when Integer
1 === Integer  # => false  — 1.=== is just ==

case uses when_value === target, so when Integer matches 1.

title: Block parameters are local
explanation:
A block parameter is local to the block. It does not overwrite the outer x.

x = 1
[2].each { |x| }  # this x is a new local
p x               # => 1

for x in [2] would assign the outer x (see the for-loop question).

title: for assigns the outer variable
code:
x = 1
for x in [2]
end
p x
explanation:
for is not a block scope. It assigns the same x that already exists:

x = 1
for x in [2]
end
p x  # => 2

[2].each { |x| } would leave the outer x as 1.

title: super vs super()
code:
class A
  def f(n)
    n
  end
end
class B < A
  def f(n)
    super()
  end
end
p B.new.f(2)
explanation:
Bare super forwards the current arguments. super() forwards none.

B.new.f(2)
super()  # calls A#f with no args — ArgumentError (given 0, expected 1)
super    # would call A#f(2) and return 2

title: == vs eql? vs equal?
code:
a = "x"
b = "x"
p [a == b, a.eql?(b), a.equal?(b)]
explanation:
== and eql? compare value. equal? compares identity (the same object).

a = "x"
b = "x"           # a second string with the same contents
a == b            # => true   value
a.eql?(b)         # => true   value (Hash uses this)
a.equal?(b)       # => false  different objects

For numbers, 1 == 1.0 is true but 1.eql?(1.0) is false, so they are different Hash keys.

title: Nested Hash#[] on a miss
explanation:
h[:a] is nil for a missing key. Then nil[:b] raises.

h = {}
h[:a]       # => nil
h[:a][:b]   # => NoMethodError  (nil has no [])

h.dig(:a, :b)  # => nil  — this is the safe walk

title: gsub! when nothing matches
code:
s = "ab"
p s.gsub!(/x/, "y")
explanation:
gsub! returns nil when it changes nothing — not the original string.

s = "ab"
s.gsub!(/x/, "y")  # => nil  (no match)
# s is still "ab"

s.gsub!(/a/, "z")  # => "zb" when it does change

Chaining s.gsub!(...).upcase blows up on nil. Use gsub (no bang) or check the return.

title: Integer divided by zero
explanation:
Integer division by zero raises.

1 / 0    # => ZeroDivisionError
1.0 / 0  # => Infinity   (Float, IEEE)

The two / operators look the same. The class of the operands decides.

title: Float divided by zero
explanation:
Float division follows IEEE 754, so dividing by 0.0 is Infinity, not an error.

1.0 / 0    # => Infinity
1 / 0      # => ZeroDivisionError  (Integer)
0.0 / 0.0  # => NaN

title: include vs prepend
code:
module M
  def hi; "M"; end
end
class A
  include M
  def hi; "A"; end
end
class B
  prepend M
  def hi; "B"; end
end
p [A.new.hi, B.new.hi]
explanation:
include puts the module behind the class. prepend puts it in front.

A.ancestors  # [A, M, ...]  so A#hi wins => "A"
B.ancestors  # [M, B, ...]  so M#hi wins => "M"

p [A.new.hi, B.new.hi]  # => ["A", "M"]

title: dup vs clone on a frozen string
code:
a = "x".freeze
p [a.dup.frozen?, a.clone.frozen?]
explanation:
clone copies freeze (and singleton methods). dup does not.

a = "x".freeze
a.dup.frozen?    # => false  — a thawed copy
a.clone.frozen?  # => true   — still frozen

Neither copies the original; both are new objects.

title: nil.to_i
code: p nil.to_i
explanation:
nil.to_i is 0, not an error. Empty string is the same:

nil.to_i  # => 0
"".to_i   # => 0
"9".to_i  # => 9

Silent 0 from a missing value is a common bug. Check for nil instead of converting it.

title: Bare rescue
code:
begin
  raise Exception.new("x")
rescue
  p :ok
end
explanation:
A bare rescue catches StandardError and its subclasses. Exception is above that, so it is not caught.

raise "x"                  # RuntimeError < StandardError — caught
raise Exception.new("x")   # not a StandardError — not caught

rescue Exception would catch it, but that also swallows NoMemoryError and Interrupt.

title: Keyword args vs a Hash
code:
def f(a:)
  a
end
p f({ a: 1 })
explanation:
Ruby 3 does not treat a positional Hash as keywords.

def f(a:)
  a
end

f({ a: 1 })  # ArgumentError — given 1 positional, missing keyword a
f(a: 1)      # => 1
f(**{ a: 1 })  # => 1  — splat makes it keywords
